primary_meaning: In Christian teaching, 'heart of the earth' is Jesus's own phrase (Matthew 12:40) prophesying His burial in the tomb/grave — the period between His death and resurrection, typologically paralleled with Jonah's three days and nights in the belly of the great fish. The dominant reading takes it as the grave itself, often with the extended sense of entering the realm of the dead (Sheol/Hades).
primary_basis: Matthew 12:40 (the source text: 'so shall the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth')
Jonah 1:17; 2:2-6 (the typological antecedent; Jonah cries 'out of the belly of Sheol')
Matthew 16:21; Luke 24:46; 1 Corinthians 15:3-4 (the 'third day' resurrection framework the phrase is read against)
Ephesians 4:9 ('descended into the lower parts of the earth')
Psalm 16:10 / Acts 2:27-31 ('you will not abandon my soul to Sheol/Hades')
1 Peter 3:18-19 (used by those extending the meaning to the descent to the dead)

alternatives.meaning: Descent into Hades/Sheol (the underworld or realm of the dead), not merely the physical tomb — the patristic and creedal reading ('He descended to the dead'), in which Christ's soul entered the abode of the dead while His body lay in the grave.

'Heart of the earth' refers to Jerusalem (viewed as the center/navel of the earth, cf. Ezekiel 5:5; 38:12), so the three days and nights begin with Jesus's betrayal/arrest and custody in the city, not with burial. This reading is advanced chiefly to resolve the chronological difficulty of fitting 'three days and three nights' between Friday burial and Sunday resurrection.
basis: Ezekiel 5:5 ('Jerusalem... in the midst/center of the nations')
Ezekiel 38:12 ('dwell at the center/navel of the earth')
Matthew 26:45-50 (delivered into the hands of sinners, taken as the starting point)

alternatives.meaning: A figurative expression for being in the grip of death and hostile powers (the 'depths' as a Hebrew idiom for extreme distress or the power of death), without a precise spatial referent — emphasizing the phrase as poetic language drawn from Jonah's psalm rather than cosmology.

Literalist chronological readings (e.g., Wednesday or Thursday crucifixion schemes) that treat 'heart of the earth' straightforwardly as the tomb but insist the 'three days and three nights' be a full 72 hours; the symbolic referent is the same (the grave) but the interpretive application differs.
basis: Matthew 12:40 read as demanding a literal 72-hour entombment
Comparison with Matthew 27:63; Mark 8:31 ('after three days')

notes: The phrase occurs only once in Scripture (Matthew 12:40), so all interpretation centers on that verse and its Jonah typology. There is broad, recognizable consensus that it refers to Jesus's burial/time in the grave, often widened to include the descent to the realm of the dead. Disagreements are mostly about scope (tomb only vs. Hades/Sheol) and chronology (when the three days and nights begin and whether they are idiomatic or literal), not about the basic referent. The 'Jerusalem as heart of the earth' reading is a genuine but distinctly minority alternative found mainly in popular apologetics and some evangelical writers addressing the chronology problem.
